extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and critics of poetry and drama (poets, dramatists, literary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetic imitation, especially Tragedy, Comedy, and Epic — covering medium, object, manner, constituent parts (plot, character, thought, diction, song, spectacle), metre, unity of time, and other formal features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three differences that distinguish modes of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic imitations (epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic, music, dance) differ in three respects: (1) the medium of imitation, (2) the objects imitated, and (3) the manner or mode of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging a work, identify and align these three dimensions: choose an appropriate medium (rhythm, language, harmony, or combination), decide whether you will represent men as better/worse/as they are, and select narration versus enacted presentation (or combinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation (rhythm, harmony, language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts employ different media: some use rhythm and harmony (music, lyre, flute), some rhythm alone (dance), some language alone (prose or verse), and some combine all (dithyrambic, nomic poetry, tragedy, comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the expressive means to the effect sought: use rhythm/harmony where musical elements dominate; use language alone when verbal argument or narrative is primary; combine where richer effects (song + speech + rhythm) are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (types of persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation represents men in action and must portray them as either better than in real life, worse than in real life, or as they are; moral character (goodness/badness) determines these divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the moral/ethical 'type' intentionally: Tragedy tends to portray nobler/higher types, Comedy the worse/lower types, and other forms may choose truth-to-life or exaggeration. Examples: Homer makes men better; Cleophon depicts them as they are; Hegemon makes them worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs dramatic presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may imitate by narration (speaking as another or in the poet's own person) or by presenting characters alive and acting; this choice shapes the work's dramatic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work will be narrative (epic often) or enacted (drama). Recognize that the same author may be of the same kind by objects (Homer vs Sophocles) yet differ by manner (narration vs enacted action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter does not alone define the poet; suitability of metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre (hexameter, iambic, elegiac, etc.) is a medium but does not by itself make the poet; the imitation (what is imitated) is decisive. Certain metres suit particular forms (hexameter for epic narrative; iambic for colloquial dialogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre for its functional appropriateness: use iambic for colloquial speech and dialogue; hexameter for extended narrative; be aware combining metres can be used but the imitation type matters more than metre alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; presented in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action (not narrative); and effects the proper purgation (catharsis) of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or assessing tragedy, check for seriousness and completeness of action, appropriate magnitude, use of embellished language (some parts in verse and some with song), enactment rather than mere narration, and whether the work arouses and purges pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and limits of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy strives, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun (unity of time); Epic action has no such temporal limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragedy, compress the action into a single day or near that limit to preserve unity and intensity; for epic, allow broader temporal scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent parts of Tragedy (and their roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy contains several constituent parts (rendered in different media): Plot (the imitation of action), Character (agents' dispositions), Thought (reasoning/ideas), Diction (choice and arrangement of words), Song/Melody, and Spectacle (stage presentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each part and their fit: plot should be primary (organizing action), character and thought should motivate actions, diction and song should suit parts of the play, and spectacle is an element but distinct from the poetic devices. Good tragedy integrates these parts coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (action over isolated episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the imitation of the action and is the central organizing principle: actions arise from agents' character and thought, and the plot should present a coherent chain of causally-related events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize a unified, causally connected plot structure where events flow from character and thought; a play with well-ordered incidents serving the action is superior to one composed of disjointed or merely spectacular episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and Thought as sources of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions spring from two natural causes—character (moral disposition) and thought (reasoning); these are what qualify and explain agents' actions within the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose dispositions and choices naturally produce the actions; ensure that thought (decisions, reasoning, intentions) is evident and aligns with resultant deeds to make the action plausible and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy — enumerated differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry and Tragedy agree in being imitations of higher characters but differ in (1) length (epic much longer; tragedy aims for compactness), (2) metre (epic uses a single metre — hexameter; tragedy uses varied metres and incorporates song), and (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epic, allow extended scope, consistent epic metre, and narrative form; when composing tragedy, constrain time/scale, employ mixed metres and song, and attend to dramatic presentation and plausibility of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of spectacle, song, and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because tragic imitation involves persons acting, spectacle (staging), song (melody), and diction (verbal arrangement) are legitimate and necessary parts of tragedy's medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spectacle to support the enacted action but not to replace the poetic/plot elements; allocate song and diction where they most enhance the emotional and rhythmic effects of the scene (some parts in verse alone, some with song).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s aim and limits (the ludicrous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates characters of a lower type; the ludicrous is a subdivision of the ugly — defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive (e.g., comic masks are ugly but not implying pain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comedy, aim to expose harmless defects and ridiculousness rather than suffering; the comic should produce laughter from incongruity or defect without cruelty that causes actual pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/technical developments as compositional guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy evolved by adding actors (from one to two to three), reducing Chorus importance, introducing scene-painting, increasing episodes, and shifting metres (iambic for dialogue replacing earlier trochaic tetrameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositional choices (number of actors, chorus role, scenic elements, episode structure, metre selection) affect dramatic form; employ them consciously to serve the plot and the desired dramatic effect rather than as mere innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative credibility and the poet’s art of plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic requires the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction — the poet must make the extraordinary seem credible within the world of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting improbable events, supply details, motivation, and internal logic that render them believable to the audience; plausibility is part of poetic truth distinct from literal factual reality.
